blocks.h2: How an Overhead Sewer System Works
blocks.body: Every drain below the street sewer's flow line, like your floor drain, a basement bathroom, or a laundry line, normally relies on gravity to reach the sewer. An overhead sewer system reroutes those drains into a sump pit instead. An [ejector pump](/hinsdale/ejector-pump) lifts that wastewater up to a line above flood level, where a check valve keeps it from flowing back down. From there, gravity carries it the rest of the way to the street sewer, the same as every drain upstairs.

blocks.intro: In June 2021, sewer water bubbled more than 5 feet high near County Line Road and Walnut Street, and a basement nearby took on about 3 feet of water.

items.body: Older homes often have deep basements and gravity floor drains. We plan the pit and pipe path around stone or brick foundations.
Many Hinsdale basements are finished to a high standard. The system is laid out to keep walls and ceilings intact where possible.
We camera your sewer before recommending a conversion. A [sewer repair](/hinsdale/sewer-repair) may solve it.

blocks.h2: Overhead Sewer Questions From Hinsdale Homeowners

items.q: Can an overhead sewer go into a finished basement?
items.answer: Yes. We plan the pit location and the pipe route to limit how much finished wall and ceiling has to open.

items.q: Does an overhead sewer stop groundwater?
items.preview: No. That's a sump pump's job.
items.answer: No. It stops sewer backups. Groundwater needs a [sump pump](/hinsdale/sump-pumps).

items.q: Can we keep the basement bathroom and bar sink?
items.answer: Yes. They drain to the new pit along with the floor drain.
Usually a few days, depending on the layout and the finishes.

items.answer: It depends on sewer depth, layout, fixtures and access. You'll approve a flat-rate price before we start.
